name: e06_signal_comparison
title: 6. Signal horse race: EMA, SMA, Faber, TSMOM, Donchian -- one bet or many?
text:
**Question.** Is EMA50/200 a special choice, or one member of a family of trend rules that all make the same bet?

**Setup.** Seven textbook long/flat rules with fixed, untuned parameters (EMA and SMA 50/200, EMA with a ±2% band, Faber's 10-month SMA, 12-month and 12-1 TSMOM, Donchian 100/50) and buy & hold, on SPY from 1994-11-28 and on 10 CORE ETFs, each on a common window after the slowest warm-up. Sharpe differences use a paired stationary bootstrap (2000 draws, 20-day blocks).

**Findings.**
- **SPY:** Sharpe ranges from 0.50 to 0.65 across the rules (best TSMOM 12M; EMA50/200 0.59, rank 6 of 7) vs 0.53 for buy & hold; max drawdowns -20% to -36% vs -55%. 4 of the 7 rules had their worst drawdown in the COVID crash, which they sat through fully invested.
- **Noise, not signal choice:** 0 of 6 Sharpe differences vs EMA50/200 have a 95% CI excluding zero; the median CI is 0.25 wide, wider than the whole 0.14 spread between the rules.
- **Across ETFs:** median Sharpe is 0.34 for buy & hold vs 0.26 (EMA50/200 ±2% band) to 0.32 (Faber 10M SMA) for the rules; EMA50/200 beats buy & hold's Sharpe in 4 of 10 ETFs. Median max drawdown falls from -60% to between -26% and -39%.
- **Same bet:** on SPY the MA and TSMOM rules' daily returns correlate 0.81-0.96 and their 0/1 exposures 0.61-0.86; across ETFs the average rule is in the same state as EMA50/200 on 86% of days. Donchian is the outlier (return correlation 0.66-0.81).
- **Trading:** the ±2% band cuts SPY round trips from 13 to 8; Faber 10M SMA and Donchian 100/50 tie for the most whipsaws (losing trips under 3 months: 7 each, compounding to -36% and -22% respectively) vs 2 for EMA50/200.
- **Trend signature:** EMA50/200 equals the sign of a weighted sum of past price changes, with weights peaking at lag 45, a mean lag of 124 days (TSMOM 12M: 125) and 11% of its weight beyond a year. The kernel reproduces the rule's state on 100.0% of SPY days (99.7% with log returns).

**Interpretation.** Levine & Pedersen (2016) show that moving-average crossovers and time-series momentum (Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen 2012) are both linear filters on past returns and are closely related once their horizons are matched; they differ mainly in the shape of the weights. The analytic kernel makes this concrete: EMA50/200 has almost the same mean lag as 12-month TSMOM (124 vs 125 days), but its weights are hump-shaped (peak at lag 45) with a long tail instead of a flat 12-month box. On SPY, EMA50/200's exposure correlates 0.73-0.86 with the other MA and TSMOM rules and 0.83 with TSMOM 12M, about as closely as with SMA50/200 (0.84) and Faber 10M SMA (0.82), whose mean lags differ by more than 30 days, so a matched horizon alone does not explain the overlap. Faber's (2007) 10-month rule weights recent changes most (mean lag 69 days) and, being checked only at month ends, trades more often than EMA50/200 on SPY (23 vs 13 round trips). Zakamulin (2014) likewise finds the real-life performance of MA and momentum timing rules far more modest than commonly reported. With highly correlated candidates and confidence intervals wider than their differences, picking "the best" rule from this table would be data snooping in the sense of Sullivan, Timmermann & White (1999): this is one trend bet, and the choice among its variants is mostly about turnover and whipsaw tolerance, not expected return. Across the 10 ETFs the family's value is risk reduction (median max drawdown -35% for EMA50/200 vs -60%), not a higher Sharpe: no variant beats buy & hold's median.
after: Correlation table: daily strategy-return correlation / daily exposure correlation (buy & hold has constant exposure, so its exposure correlation is undefined). Kernel weights are on daily price changes and scaled to sum to one; Faber's monthly rule is approximated by a daily 210-bar SMA, and Donchian, being path-dependent, has no linear kernel.
